title: Starting a Business · Episode 3
chapters: Double-entry bookkeeping: the Renaissance idea behind every business
Lessons from startup wins and flops

units.t: Starting a Business. Episode three.
In this episode: Double-entry bookkeeping: the Renaissance idea behind every business, Starting a business in Australia and Lessons from startup wins and flops.
Part one. Double-entry bookkeeping: the Renaissance idea behind every business.
A friar who was friends with Leonardo da Vinci wrote down a method that still sits beneath every company's accounts, from corner cafes to global giants.
A system for merchants.
Picture a merchant in fourteenth-century Genoa, Florence or Venice.
He buys wool on credit, ships cloth to distant ports, borrows from partners and lends to customers.
A simple list of money in and out no longer shows whether he is making a profit, who owes him and whom he owes.
Italian merchants and bankers gradually developed a cleverer method.
Surviving account books show it in use by at least the 1300s, and houses like the Medici bank relied on it.
Nobody knows who invented it.
In 1494 the friar and mathematician Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo da Vinci, published a huge textbook in Venice with a section on merchants' bookkeeping.
Printing spread it across Europe.
He described the system rather than inventing it, stressing careful daily records and books that balance.
Every transaction has two sides.
The core idea is simple and powerful.
Every business transaction affects at least two things, so you record it twice.
Suppose a small business buys a delivery van for 20,000 dollars in cash.
It gains a van but loses the same amount of cash.
Both changes are written down.
If it instead borrows 20,000 dollars from a bank, it gains cash and also gains a debt to repay.
Recording both sides means nothing slips through the cracks.
Money never just appears or vanishes in the books; it always comes from somewhere and goes somewhere.
This also creates a built-in error check, because if the two sides do not match, a mistake has been made.
The accounting equation.
Double-entry rests on one balancing rule, the accounting equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity.
Assets are what the business owns or controls, such as cash, stock, equipment and money customers owe it.
Liabilities are what it owes others, such as loans and unpaid bills.
Equity is what is left for the owners, including the money they put in and the profits kept in the business.
The equation says that everything a business has was funded either by borrowing or by its owners.
Because every transaction is recorded on both sides, the equation stays true after each one.
The balance sheet, one of a company's main financial reports, is this equation set out in detail.
Debits and credits.
The words debit and credit confuse almost everyone at first, because in daily life a credit sounds good and a debit sounds bad.
In bookkeeping they just mean the left side and the right side of an account.
By convention, debits increase assets and expenses, while credits increase liabilities, equity and income.
Every transaction must have equal debits and credits.
This explains why your bank statement seems backwards.
When you deposit money, the bank records a credit to your account, because from the bank's point of view your money is something it owes you, a liability.
The language is written from the perspective of whoever keeps the books.
Why it still matters.
More than five centuries after Pacioli, accounting software still runs on double-entry under the surface.
When an app shows a profit figure, a balance sheet or an amount owing for tax, it builds those reports from paired entries.
The method made larger, more complex businesses possible, because owners could track performance without personally watching every coin.
It also let outsiders such as banks and investors judge a business from its accounts.
Some historians argue it helped shape modern capitalism itself, though that bigger claim is debated.
The German writer Goethe had a character call it one of the finest inventions of the human mind.
For anyone starting a business, understanding it is a genuine superpower.
The key idea: Double-entry bookkeeping evolved among Italian merchants and was described in print by Luca Pacioli in 1494.
Part two. Starting a business in Australia.
ABN, ASIC, GST, sole trader or company: the paperwork sounds daunting, but the basic steps are simpler than most people think.
Business or hobby.
Not every side activity is a business.
The ATO considers whether you intend to make a profit, whether the activity is repeated and regular, whether it's organised in a business-like way, and its size.
Selling a few of your own paintings each year may be a hobby; producing them regularly for sale, marketing them and keeping records looks like a business.
The distinction matters for tax: business income is generally taxable and business expenses may be deductible.
The ATO and business.
gov.
au both have guidance to help you decide.
Structure and liability.
Your structure affects your tax, legal duties and personal risk.
A sole trader is the simplest and cheapest: you and the business are legally the same, you use your own tax file number, and profit is taxed at personal rates.
A partnership is two or more people sharing profits.
A company is a separate legal entity.
Trusts are often used for family businesses.
You can change structure later, though it may cost money.
The biggest difference is liability.
A sole trader is personally responsible for all business debts, so a house and savings could be at risk.
Partners are generally liable for the whole partnership's debts.
A company offers limited liability, though directors can still be personally liable in some situations, such as trading while insolvent.
Companies cost more and need ASIC registration.
ABN and business names.
Most people starting out apply for an Australian Business Number, an 11-digit number that identifies your business.
Applying is free through the Australian Business Register, reachable via business.
gov.
au.
Beware of third-party sites charging fees for the same thing.
You need an ABN to register a business name and for GST.
Without one, businesses paying you may have to withhold tax at the top marginal rate.
If you trade as Sarah Nguyen, you needn't register a name.
If you trade as 'Northside Dog Walking', you generally must register it with ASIC, for one or three years, for a fee.
It doesn't give you exclusive ownership; a trade mark through IP Australia does.
Check the name and a matching domain are available first.
GST registration.
Goods and services tax is a 10% tax on most goods and services in Australia.
You must register when your annual GST turnover reaches $75,000, or $150,000 for non-profit organisations.
Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must register regardless of turnover.
Once registered, you generally add GST to your prices, lodge a business activity statement, or BAS, and pass the GST you collect to the ATO, minus GST credits on your business purchases.
You can register voluntarily below the threshold; whether that's worthwhile depends on your customers and costs.
Licences, records, first steps.
Depending on your industry and location, you may need licences or permits, from food handling to building work.
ABLIS, on business.
gov.
au, helps you find them.
If you employ staff, workers' compensation insurance is compulsory and you must pay super.
Public liability and professional indemnity insurance aren't always required, but are common.
The ATO generally requires business records to be kept for five years.
A sensible order: check you're really in business, choose a structure, get an ABN, register a name if needed, consider GST.
Open a separate business bank account from day one and set up simple accounting software.
Business.
gov.
au is a free, reliable starting point.
This is general information only: rules change, so talk to a registered tax agent, accountant or lawyer.
The key idea: The ATO looks at intention to profit, regularity and business-like behaviour to decide whether you're in business.
Part three. Lessons from startup wins and flops.
Canva was rejected by investors again and again.
Juicero raised over $100 million and vanished.
What separates them is rarely luck alone.
Canva and Atlassian.
In 2007, Melanie Perkins, then a Perth university student, noticed how hard design software was to learn.
With Cliff Obrecht she started Fusion Books, an online tool for school yearbooks, run from her mother's lounge room.
Pitching a broader platform, Perkins has said she was rejected by around 100 investors.
With Cameron Adams, she launched Canva in 2013.
It is now one of the world's most valuable start-ups.
Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar met at UNSW and founded Atlassian in Sydney in 2002, reportedly with about $10,000 on a credit card.
Their early product Jira helped software teams track bugs.
They grew for years without a traditional sales team, relying on transparent prices and word of mouth.
Atlassian listed on Nasdaq in 2015.
Product-market fit.
Investor Marc Andreessen popularised the term in a 2007 essay, describing it as being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market.
You can often feel it: customers use the product eagerly, tell others and complain loudly when it breaks.
Growth marketer Sean Ellis proposed a simple test.
Ask users how they'd feel if they could no longer use your product.
If around 40% or more say 'very disappointed', you may be close.
Before fit, focus on learning; after it, on growing.
Juicero and Quibi.
Juicero launched in 2016 with a Wi-Fi-connected juice press that initially sold for about US$700, later cut to about US$400, and used proprietary juice packs.
It raised roughly US$120 million.
In 2017, Bloomberg reporters showed the packs could be squeezed by hand to produce much the same juice.
It shut down that year.
A sophisticated solution must deliver real value beyond the simplest alternative.
Quibi, a phone streaming service led by Jeffrey Katzenberg, raised about US$1.
75 billion, launched in April 2020 and shut down about six months later.
Observers cited COVID-19 lockdowns, hard-to-share clips and free rivals like YouTube and TikTok.
Money can't substitute for testing whether customers want the product.
Why startups fail.
Research firm CB Insights has analysed post-mortems written by founders of failed startups.
In its widely cited reports, 'no market need' and 'ran out of cash' rank among the most common reasons, alongside being outcompeted, pricing problems and team issues.
The reasons are self-reported, so the data isn't perfect.
Still, the pattern fits experience.
Building something people don't need is the most common and most avoidable mistake.
Running out of money is often the final symptom rather than the root cause.
Pivot, persist, learn.
A pivot is a structured change of strategy that keeps what you've learned.
Slack emerged from a company building an online game called Glitch; the game failed, but its internal chat tool became the product.
Instagram began as Burbn, a check-in app, before its founders focused on the photo-sharing people actually used.
YouTube's founders have said it was first pitched as a video dating site.
The hard judgement is when to persist and when to pivot.
Let customer behaviour, not pride or sunk costs, decide.
Talk to customers early, launch small, and watch your runway.
Remember survivorship bias: for every famous success, many similar companies failed.
Success stories show what's possible, not what's guaranteed.
The key idea: Canva and Atlassian solved real, widespread problems, and Atlassian grew by letting a good product sell itself.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Pacioli's 1494 book do for bookkeeping?
Answer. Spread an existing method across Europe.
Question two. Which activity is most likely to look like a business rather than a hobby?
Answer. Making paintings regularly to sell, with records.
Question three. What did Atlassian do unusually in its early years?
Answer. Grew for years without a traditional sales team.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
